topics.name: Characteristics and classification of living organisms

questions.q: Which is one of the seven characteristics of living things?
questions.why: MRS GREN: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition.

questions.q: In the binomial system, what are the two parts of a name?
questions.why: For example Homo sapiens: genus Homo, species sapiens.

questions.q: Which group has a body made of segments with jointed legs and an exoskeleton?
questions.why: Arthropods (insects, crustaceans, arachnids, myriapods) have jointed legs and an exoskeleton.

questions.q: An animal has dry scaly skin, breathes with lungs and lays eggs with rubbery shells on land. Which vertebrate group does it belong to?
questions.why: Dry scales and rubbery-shelled eggs laid on land are features of reptiles. Amphibians have moist skin and lay eggs in water, birds have feathers, and fish have gills.

questions.q: Two species have very similar base sequences in their DNA. What does this most likely show?
o: They share a recent common ancestor
They live in the same habitat
questions.why: The more recently two groups shared an ancestor, the more similar their DNA base sequences are, so DNA comparisons are used in classification.

long.q: Explain why viruses are not considered living organisms by biologists.
scheme: B1: viruses lack cellular structure (no cytoplasm, cell membrane, or organelles)
B1: they do not carry out metabolic processes or respiration on their own
B1: they cannot reproduce independently; they can only replicate inside a host cell by hijacking the host's machinery
B1: they do not feed, excrete, or grow

long.q: A student says a car is alive because it moves, uses fuel and gives out waste gases. Using the characteristics of living organisms, give three reasons why the car is not a living organism.
scheme: B1: it does not grow (no permanent increase in size or dry mass)
B1: it cannot reproduce / make more cars like itself
B1: it is not sensitive: it cannot detect or respond to changes in its environment by itself (or: it does not respire / is not made of cells)

long.q: The lion is named Panthera leo and the tiger Panthera tigris. Describe what is meant by the binomial system of naming and state what these two names show about the lion and the tiger.
scheme: B1: an internationally agreed system in which each species is given a scientific name in two parts
B1: the first part is the genus and the second part is the species (Panthera is the genus)
B1: lion and tiger are in the same genus but are different species, so they are closely related

long.q: An animal has a hard exoskeleton, three pairs of jointed legs, two pairs of wings and a body in three parts. Name the phylum and the class it belongs to, and state two features that would show an animal in the same phylum is a crustacean instead.
scheme: B1: phylum: arthropods
B1: class: insects
B1: a crustacean has more than four pairs of jointed legs
B1: a crustacean has two pairs of antennae (and a body in two parts: cephalothorax and abdomen)

long.q: Scientists now often classify organisms by comparing the base sequences of their DNA. Explain why this method is used and what it shows when two species have very similar sequences.
scheme: B1: DNA base sequences (and the amino acid sequences of proteins they code for) change over time and reflect evolutionary relationships
B1: species with more similar base sequences share a more recent common ancestor, so they are more closely related
B1: it is more reliable than comparing body features, because similar features can appear in organisms that are not closely related

questions.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but not animal cells?
questions.why: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall (and often chloroplasts and a large vacuole).

questions.q: Where does aerobic respiration take place in a cell?
questions.why: Mitochondria release energy by aerobic respiration.

questions.q: An image is 50 mm long; magnification is ×500. What is the actual size?
questions.why: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 50 ÷ 500 = 0.1 mm.

questions.q: A group of similar cells working together is a…
questions.why: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.

questions.q: Which of these cells contain chloroplasts?
o: Both root hair and palisade mesophyll cells
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some believed root hair cells have chloroplasts. They are underground and do not photosynthesise.

long.q: State three structures found in a palisade mesophyll cell that are not found in a liver cell, and give the function of each.
scheme: B1: cell wall
B1: cell wall strengthens the cell / gives support / stops it bursting when it takes in water
B1: chloroplasts
B1: chloroplasts absorb light energy for photosynthesis
B1: large permanent vacuole
B1: vacuole contains cell sap / keeps the cell turgid

long.q: A photomicrograph shows a human cheek cell at a magnification of ×400. The image of the cell is 24 mm wide. Calculate the actual width of the cell in micrometres (µm).
scheme: M1: actual size = image size ÷ magnification

long.q: State the function of each of these specialised cells: a root hair cell, a neurone, a sperm cell and a palisade mesophyll cell.
scheme: B1: root hair cell: absorption of water and mineral ions from the soil
B1: neurone: conducting electrical impulses
B1: sperm cell: reproduction, fertilising an egg cell
B1: palisade mesophyll cell: photosynthesis

long.q: Define the terms tissue and organ, and give one example of each from a flowering plant.
scheme: B1: tissue: a group of cells with similar structures, working together to perform a shared function
B1: plant tissue example, e.g. xylem, phloem, palisade mesophyll or epidermis
B1: organ: a structure made of a group of tissues working together to perform specific functions
B1: plant organ example, e.g. leaf, root, stem or flower

long.q: Cells in the pancreas make and secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes. Explain why these cells contain a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and many mitochondria.
scheme: B1: ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis and enzymes are proteins
B1: rough endoplasmic reticulum is covered in ribosomes, so a lot of it gives many sites for making enzymes
B1: mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy
B1: making and secreting proteins needs a lot of energy, so many mitochondria are needed

topics.name: Movement into and out of cells

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of…
o: any molecules down a concentration gradient
water through a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution
questions.why: Osmosis is the net movement of water from a higher to a lower water potential across a partially permeable membrane.

questions.q: Which process needs energy from respiration?
questions.why: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, using energy.

questions.q: A plant cell is put in concentrated salt solution. What happens?
o: It loses water and becomes plasmolysed
It gains water and becomes turgid
questions.why: Water leaves by osmosis; the cytoplasm pulls away from the cell wall.

questions.q: A dialysis tubing bag of sucrose solution is placed in water. The bag gets heavier. What has happened?
o: Net movement of water into the bag by osmosis
Net movement of sucrose out of the bag
Diffusion of sucrose into the water
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought sucrose moved out. Sucrose molecules are too large to pass through; water moves in by osmosis.

questions.q: What is active transport across a biological membrane?
o: Movement of water down a water potential gradient
Movement of particles against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration
Diffusion through open protein channels without energy
questions.why: Active transport moves substances from low to high concentration across a cell membrane using carrier proteins and ATP energy.

long.q: Define osmosis and explain why potato strips placed in a concentrated sugar solution lose mass.
scheme: B1: the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane
B1: the solution has a lower water potential than the potato cells
B1: so water leaves the cells by osmosis

long.q: Define diffusion and state two factors that increase the rate of diffusion.
scheme: B1: the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration (down a concentration gradient), as a result of their random movement
B1: one factor, e.g. a larger surface area or a steeper concentration gradient
B1: a second different factor, e.g. a higher temperature or a shorter distance

long.q: Root hair cells absorb nitrate ions from soil water even though the concentration of nitrate ions in the soil water is lower than inside the cells. Name the process, explain how it happens, and explain why uptake stops if the soil becomes waterlogged and short of oxygen.
scheme: B1: active transport
B1: ions move from a lower to a higher concentration, against the concentration gradient
B1: carried by protein carriers in the cell membrane
B1: it needs energy released by respiration
B1: without oxygen there is little aerobic respiration in the root cells, so not enough energy is released for active transport

long.q: A student puts carrot cylinders into sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 30 minutes. One cylinder changed from 2.50 g to 2.20 g. Calculate its percentage change in mass, explain why percentage change is used rather than change in mass, and state two variables the student should keep constant.
scheme: M1: change in mass = 2.20 − 2.50 = −0.30 g, divided by the starting mass 2.50 g, × 100
A1: −12% (a 12% decrease)
B1: the cylinders may start with different masses, so percentage change allows a fair comparison
B1: one controlled variable, e.g. same volume of solution or same temperature
B1: a second controlled variable, e.g. same time in solution or same size/surface area of cylinders

long.q: Describe and explain what happens to plant cells placed in pure water and to plant cells placed in a concentrated salt solution, and explain why turgid cells are important to a plant.
scheme: B1: in pure water, water enters the cells by osmosis and the vacuole swells, so the cell becomes turgid
B1: the inelastic cell wall pushes back (turgor pressure), stopping the cell from bursting
B1: in concentrated salt solution, water leaves by osmosis and the cytoplasm and membrane shrink away from the cell wall (plasmolysis)
B1: turgid cells press against each other and support the plant; if they lose water the plant wilts

questions.q: Which test detects starch?
questions.why: Iodine turns blue-black with starch.

questions.q: What are proteins made from?
questions.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

questions.q: Benedict's solution is heated with a sample and turns brick red. What is present?
questions.why: Reducing sugars give a green to brick-red colour with hot Benedict's.

questions.q: In a DNA molecule, which base always pairs with adenine (A)?
questions.why: The bases on the two strands pair in a fixed way: A with T and C with G. Uracil is not found in DNA.

questions.q: A food sample is shaken with ethanol and the liquid is then poured into water. A cloudy white emulsion forms. What does the food contain?
questions.why: A cloudy white emulsion in the ethanol emulsion test shows fats or oils are present. Starch, protein and reducing sugar are tested with iodine, biuret and Benedict's solution.

long.q: Describe how a student could test a solution of fruit juice for reducing sugars and state the positive result.
scheme: B1: add an equal volume of Benedict's solution to the juice
B1: heat in a hot water bath (about 80 °C) for a few minutes
B1: positive result: colour changes from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick red

long.q: Describe how a student could test a sample of milk for protein and for fat, stating the positive result of each test.
scheme: B1: protein: add biuret solution (or sodium hydroxide then dilute copper(II) sulfate) to the milk
B1: protein present: blue changes to purple/violet
B1: fat: shake the sample with ethanol, then pour the liquid into water
B1: fat present: a cloudy white emulsion forms

long.q: Name the smaller molecules that starch, proteins and fats are made from, and state the chemical elements found in carbohydrates and in proteins.
scheme: B1: starch is made from glucose
B1: proteins are made from amino acids
B1: fats and oils are made from fatty acids and glycerol
B1: carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
B1: proteins contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (and sometimes sulfur)

long.q: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule.
scheme: B1: two strands coiled together to form a double helix
B1: each strand contains chemicals called bases (A, T, C and G)
B1: bonds between pairs of bases hold the two strands together
B1: bases always pair the same way: A with T and C with G

long.q: A section of double-stranded DNA contains 1200 bases in total. 18% of the bases are adenine (A). Calculate the number of guanine (G) bases in this section.
scheme: M1: A pairs with T, so thymine is also 18%
M1: C + G = 100 − 36 = 64%, and C pairs with G so G = 32%
A1: 0.32 × 1200 = 384 guanine bases

questions.q: What is an enzyme?
o: A protein that acts as a biological catalyst
questions.why: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions without being used up.

questions.q: Why does an enzyme stop working at high temperatures?
o: Its active site changes shape (it is denatured)
questions.why: Heat breaks bonds holding its shape, so the substrate no longer fits the active site.

questions.q: What does amylase break down?
questions.why: Amylase digests starch into simple sugars (maltose).

questions.q: Which statement about enzymes is correct?
o: All enzymes work best at pH 7
Enzymes are used up in reactions
Different enzymes have different optimum pH values
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many believed all enzymes are most effective at pH 7; pepsin in the stomach works best near pH 2.

questions.q: Why does the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction drop to zero at very high temperatures?
o: Substrate molecules run out of kinetic energy
The enzyme's active site denatures as bonds maintaining tertiary structure break
questions.why: Excess thermal energy breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds, distorting the active site shape so the substrate can no longer bind.

long.q: Explain why the activity of an enzyme falls when the temperature rises above its optimum.
scheme: B1: the enzyme is denatured
B1: the shape of the active site changes
B1: so the substrate no longer fits / is no longer complementary, and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form

long.q: Define the terms catalyst and enzyme, and explain why enzymes are important to living organisms.
scheme: B1: catalyst: a substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is not changed by the reaction
B1: enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts
B1: they speed up reactions in cells so that the reactions are fast enough to sustain life

long.q: Explain why the enzyme amylase can break down starch but cannot break down protein.
scheme: B1: each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape
B1: the shape of a starch molecule is complementary to the active site of amylase, so they form an enzyme–substrate complex
B1: protein molecules are not complementary to (do not fit) the active site, so no complex forms and no reaction happens

long.q: Describe how a student could use amylase, starch suspension, iodine solution, buffer solutions and a spotting tile to investigate the effect of pH on the activity of amylase.
scheme: B1: mix a fixed volume of starch suspension with a buffer of one pH and leave it in a water bath at a fixed temperature (e.g. 37 °C)
B1: add a fixed volume of amylase and start a timer
B1: at regular intervals (e.g. every 30 s) add a drop of the mixture to a drop of iodine solution on the spotting tile
B1: record the time when the iodine no longer turns blue-black (stays orange-brown), showing all the starch has been digested
B1: repeat with buffers across a range of pH values, e.g. pH 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8
B1: keep temperature and the volumes and concentrations of starch and amylase the same, and repeat each pH to calculate a mean

long.q: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increases as the temperature is raised from 10 °C to 30 °C.
scheme: B1: enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster
B1: so they collide more often (more effective collisions)
B1: more enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time, so the rate increases

questions.q: What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
questions.why: Light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll, converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

questions.q: Which mineral ion is needed to make chlorophyll?
questions.why: Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule; a lack causes yellow leaves.

questions.q: Gas exchange in a leaf happens mainly through…
questions.why: Stomata, opened and closed by guard cells, let gases in and out.

questions.q: What is the balanced equation for plant photosynthesis?
questions.why: Six molecules of carbon dioxide and six molecules of water yield one molecule of glucose and six molecules of oxygen gas.

questions.q: Increasing the light intensity on a plant does not change its rate of photosynthesis, but raising the carbon dioxide concentration makes the rate go up. What was limiting the rate?
questions.why: A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply: only changing it changes the rate. Here only the carbon dioxide increase raised the rate, so carbon dioxide was limiting.

long.q: Write the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis and explain why increasing light intensity stops increasing the rate of photosynthesis above a certain point.
scheme: B1: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (light, chlorophyll)
B1: another factor becomes limiting
B1: e.g. carbon dioxide concentration or temperature

long.q: Describe the steps required to test a green leaf for the presence of starch, explaining the purpose of each step.
scheme: B1: boil the leaf in water for 1-2 minutes to kill the leaf cells and disrupt the cell membranes
B1: turn off the Bunsen burner, then warm the leaf in ethanol in a water bath to dissolve and remove the green chlorophyll
B1: dip the brittle leaf into warm water to soften it
B1: spread the leaf on a white tile and add drops of iodine solution
B1: a blue-black colour shows starch is present; it stays yellow-brown if not
long.ans: Blue-black for positive; yellow-brown for negative

long.q: Explain how the structure of a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis.
scheme: B1: large surface area to absorb as much light as possible
B1: thin, so a short diffusion distance for carbon dioxide to reach the cells
B1: palisade mesophyll cells near the upper surface are packed with chloroplasts to absorb most light
B1: air spaces in the spongy mesophyll let carbon dioxide diffuse to the cells
B1: stomata let carbon dioxide in (and oxygen out), and xylem in the veins brings water

long.q: Explain why a plant growing in soil short of nitrate ions, and a plant growing in soil short of magnesium ions, each grow poorly.
scheme: B1: nitrate ions are needed to make amino acids and so proteins
B1: nitrate deficiency: poor, stunted growth (often with yellowing older leaves), because too little protein is made for new cells
B1: magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll
B1: magnesium deficiency: yellowing of leaves (chlorosis), so less light is absorbed and less photosynthesis happens

long.q: A student investigates the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis by placing a lamp at different distances from a piece of pondweed and counting the bubbles of gas given off. State the independent and dependent variables, two variables to control, and one improvement to the method with a reason.
scheme: B1: independent variable: distance of the lamp from the pondweed (light intensity)
B1: dependent variable: number of bubbles per minute
B1: control temperature, e.g. with a water bath or a heat shield of water between lamp and plant, since the lamp gives off heat
B1: control carbon dioxide concentration (same concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate) or use the same piece of pondweed
B1: collect the gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder and measure its volume, because bubbles can be different sizes

questions.q: Where is bile made?
questions.why: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

questions.q: What does bile do?
o: Emulsifies fats and neutralises stomach acid
questions.why: Bile breaks fat into small droplets (bigger surface area) and is alkaline.

questions.q: Where are most digested nutrients absorbed?
questions.why: The ileum has villi giving a huge surface area for absorption.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a lack of vitamin C?
questions.why: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy; vitamin D deficiency causes rickets.

questions.q: What are the functions of the hydrochloric acid in gastric juice?
o: It kills harmful microorganisms in food and gives an acidic pH for stomach enzymes
It digests starch and emulsifies fats
It neutralises bile and absorbs glucose
It makes bile and stores glycogen
questions.why: Stomach acid kills many microorganisms swallowed with food and provides the low pH that the protease pepsin works best at. It does not digest food itself.

long.q: State the importance in the diet of vitamin C, vitamin D, calcium, iron and dietary fibre.
scheme: B1: vitamin C: needed to make collagen / prevents scurvy
B1: vitamin D: helps absorption of calcium for bones and teeth / prevents rickets
B1: calcium: for strong bones and teeth
B1: iron: to make haemoglobin in red blood cells
B1: fibre: helps peristalsis / prevents constipation

long.q: Explain how the villi of the small intestine are adapted for the absorption of digested food.
scheme: B1: villi (and microvilli) greatly increase the surface area for absorption
B1: the wall is one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
B1: a dense network of capillaries carries absorbed glucose and amino acids away, keeping a steep concentration gradient
B1: a lacteal in each villus absorbs fatty acids and glycerol

long.q: Describe the roles of bile and lipase in the digestion of fats.
scheme: B1: bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder
B1: bile neutralises the acidic mixture from the stomach, giving a suitable pH for enzymes in the small intestine
B1: bile emulsifies fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase
B1: lipase breaks fats down into fatty acids and glycerol

long.q: Describe the roles of hydrochloric acid in the stomach and name the proteases that digest protein in the stomach and in the small intestine.
scheme: B1: hydrochloric acid kills harmful microorganisms in food
B1: it gives an acidic pH, the optimum for pepsin
B1: pepsin in the stomach and trypsin (from the pancreas) in the small intestine
B1: these proteases break protein down into amino acids

long.q: Explain the difference between physical (mechanical) digestion and chemical digestion, and describe the role of teeth in digestion.
scheme: B1: physical digestion breaks food into smaller pieces without chemical change to the food molecules
B1: this increases the surface area for enzymes to act on
B1: chemical digestion uses enzymes to break large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules
B1: incisors cut and bite food; premolars and molars crush and grind it

questions.q: What does xylem carry?
questions.why: Xylem transports water and mineral ions up from the roots.

questions.q: Which conditions increase the rate of transpiration?
questions.why: Higher temperature and wind speed and lower humidity all speed up water loss.

questions.q: Translocation in phloem moves…
questions.why: Phloem moves sucrose and amino acids from sources to sinks.

questions.q: Which tissue transports sucrose and amino acids in a plant?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many did not understand the functions of xylem (water and ions) and phloem (sucrose and amino acids).

questions.q: Why do root hair cells have a long, thin extension into the soil?
o: To anchor the plant firmly in the soil
To transport sucrose down to the root tip
To increase the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions
questions.why: The extension gives each root hair cell a large surface area in contact with soil water, so more water (by osmosis) and mineral ions can be taken in.

long.q: Explain how transpiration in leaves produces a continuous flow of water upwards through the xylem of a plant.
scheme: B1: water evaporates from the moist surfaces of mesophyll cells into the air spaces within the leaf
B1: water vapour diffuses out through open stomata down a water vapour concentration gradient
B1: this water loss creates a low water potential in the mesophyll cells, drawing water out of the leaf xylem by osmosis
B1: this creates a negative pressure / transpiration pull that draws water up the xylem vessels
B1: cohesion between polar water molecules forms a continuous unbroken water column up the stem from the roots

long.q: State the functions of xylem and phloem in a plant, including the direction in which each transports substances.
scheme: B1: xylem transports water and mineral ions
B1: xylem carries them upwards, from the roots to the leaves
B1: phloem transports sucrose and amino acids
B1: phloem carries them both up and down the plant

long.q: Explain how an increase in temperature and an increase in humidity each affect the rate of transpiration.
scheme: B1: higher temperature increases the rate of transpiration
B1: water molecules have more kinetic energy, so evaporation from mesophyll cells and diffusion of water vapour out of the leaf are faster
B1: higher humidity decreases the rate of transpiration
B1: there is a smaller water vapour concentration gradient between the air spaces in the leaf and the air outside, so diffusion out of the stomata is slower

long.q: A student uses a potometer to measure water uptake by a leafy shoot. Explain why the shoot is cut and fitted under water, describe how to compare still air with moving air, and calculate the rate of water uptake if the air bubble moves 36 mm along a capillary tube of cross-sectional area 0.8 mm² in 4 minutes.
scheme: B1: cutting and fitting under water stops air entering the xylem, which would break the water column (and joints are sealed to stop leaks)
B1: measure how far the bubble moves in a set time in still air
B1: then repeat with a fan at a fixed distance, keeping light intensity and temperature the same
M1: volume = 36 × 0.8 = 28.8 mm³
A1: rate = 28.8 ÷ 4 = 7.2 mm³ per minute

long.q: Explain why a potato tuber acts as a sink for sucrose in summer but as a source of sucrose in spring.
scheme: B1: translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources to sinks
B1: in summer, sucrose made in the leaves is transported to the tuber, where it is converted to starch and stored, so the tuber is a sink
B1: in spring, before new leaves can photosynthesise, the stored starch is broken down to sucrose
B1: this sucrose is transported in the phloem to the growing shoots, so the tuber is now a source

questions.q: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart at high pressure?
questions.why: Arteries have thick, elastic walls to carry high-pressure blood from the heart.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood to the body?
questions.why: The left ventricle has the thickest wall and pumps blood round the whole body.

questions.q: What is the job of red blood cells?
questions.why: Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues.

questions.q: Why does the heart rate rise during exercise?
o: To supply muscles with more oxygen and glucose and remove carbon dioxide
questions.why: Working muscles respire faster and need faster delivery and removal.

questions.q: Which vessels carry blood away from the heart?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought veins take blood away from the heart. Arteries carry blood away; veins return it.

long.q: Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle.
scheme: B1: the left ventricle pumps blood all around the body (the right only to the lungs)
B1: so it needs more muscle to create a higher pressure

long.q: Describe the double circulation of a mammal and explain one advantage of it.
scheme: B1: blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body
B1: the right side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs, and it returns to the left side
B1: the left side pumps blood to the rest of the body
B1: advantage: blood returning from the lungs can be pumped again at high pressure, so oxygen is delivered to the body quickly (while lower pressure protects the lungs)

long.q: State the functions of red blood cells, phagocytes, lymphocytes, platelets and plasma.
scheme: B1: red blood cells: transport oxygen (as oxyhaemoglobin)
B1: phagocytes: engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis)
B1: lymphocytes: produce antibodies
B1: platelets: help the blood to clot
B1: plasma: transports blood cells, ions, nutrients (e.g. glucose), urea, hormones and carbon dioxide

long.q: Explain how the structures of arteries, veins and capillaries are related to their functions.
scheme: B1: arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls
B1: so they withstand and maintain the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart
B1: veins have thin walls and a wide lumen, as blood is at low pressure
B1: veins have valves to prevent backflow of blood
B1: capillary walls are one cell thick
B1: giving a short diffusion distance for exchange of substances with tissues

long.q: Describe how coronary heart disease develops and state two risk factors for it.
scheme: B1: the coronary arteries become narrowed or blocked by fatty deposits (cholesterol)
B1: less blood reaches the heart muscle, so it gets less oxygen and glucose; part of it may stop working or die (heart attack)
B1: one risk factor, e.g. a diet high in saturated fat, smoking, stress or lack of exercise
B1: a second different risk factor, e.g. genetic factors, increasing age or being male

questions.q: What is a pathogen?
questions.why: Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protoctists that cause disease.

questions.q: How does a vaccine protect you?
o: It makes your body produce antibodies and memory cells
It removes pathogens from the blood
questions.why: Harmless antigens trigger an immune response, leaving memory cells for a faster future response.

questions.q: Why don't antibiotics work against viral infections?
o: Viruses don't have the structures antibiotics target
Viruses are not living cells, so antibiotics kill them instantly
questions.why: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures (like cell walls) that viruses don't have.

questions.q: Which of these is a chemical barrier against pathogens?
questions.why: Stomach acid (and mucus) are chemical barriers. Skin and nose hairs are mechanical barriers, and phagocytes are white blood cells, not barriers.

questions.q: A baby receives antibodies from its mother in breast milk. Why does this protection only last a short time?
o: Breast milk also contains antibiotics that wear off
No memory cells are made, because the baby's own immune system did not make the antibodies
The baby's stomach acid destroys every antibody at once
questions.why: This is passive immunity: the antibodies are made by someone else, so the baby's lymphocytes make no memory cells and the antibodies are broken down over time.

long.q: Define the terms pathogen and transmissible disease, and describe two ways in which pathogens can be transmitted.
scheme: B1: pathogen: a disease-causing organism
B1: transmissible disease: a disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another
B1: direct contact, e.g. through blood or other body fluids
B1: indirect contact, e.g. contaminated surfaces, food, animals or the air (droplets)

long.q: Describe four ways in which the body stops pathogens getting in or kills them before they can cause disease, without using white blood cells.
scheme: B1: skin acts as a barrier
B1: hairs in the nose trap particles carrying pathogens
B1: mucus traps pathogens in the airways (and cilia move it away)
B1: stomach acid kills pathogens in food

long.q: Explain how vaccination gives long-term protection against a disease.
scheme: B1: the vaccine contains weakened or harmless pathogens, or their antigens
B1: the antigens stimulate lymphocytes (with complementary receptors) to divide
B1: the lymphocytes produce specific antibodies
B1: memory cells are produced and stay in the body
B1: on later infection, memory cells give a faster and larger antibody response, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms develop

long.q: Compare active and passive immunity, using a breast-fed baby as an example of passive immunity.
scheme: B1: active immunity: the body makes its own antibodies after meeting an antigen (by infection or vaccination)
B1: passive immunity: antibodies are received from another individual, e.g. a baby gets antibodies in breast milk (or across the placenta)
B1: passive immunity is short-term because the antibodies are broken down and no memory cells are made
B1: active immunity is long-term because memory cells are made

long.q: Describe how antibodies protect the body, and explain why antibodies made against one pathogen do not protect against a different pathogen.
scheme: B1: antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes
B1: they bind to antigens on the pathogen
B1: this leads to the pathogen being destroyed directly, or marks it for destruction by phagocytes
B1: each antibody has a shape complementary to one specific antigen
B1: a different pathogen has different antigens, so the antibody cannot bind to it

questions.q: Where does gas exchange happen in the lungs?
questions.why: Alveoli have thin walls, a large surface area and a good blood supply.

questions.q: When you breathe in, the diaphragm…
questions.why: Contracting flattens it, increasing chest volume and drawing air in.

questions.q: Exhaled air contains more ___ than inhaled air.
questions.why: Exhaled air has about 4% CO₂ compared with about 0.04% in inhaled air.

questions.q: Which feature makes the alveoli efficient at gas exchange?
o: Walls only one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
questions.why: Thin alveolar walls, a large surface area and a good blood supply keep the diffusion distance short and the concentration gradients steep.

questions.q: When the external intercostal muscles contract as you breathe in, what happens inside the thorax?
questions.why: The ribs move up and out, so the volume of the thorax increases and the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure, and air is drawn in.

long.q: State four features of the gas exchange surface in humans that make gas exchange efficient.
scheme: B1: large surface area
B1: thin surface, giving a short diffusion distance
B1: good blood supply
B1: good ventilation with air

long.q: Describe how the intercostal muscles and the diaphragm cause air to enter the lungs when you breathe in.
scheme: B1: the external intercostal muscles contract
B1: the ribcage moves upwards and outwards
B1: the diaphragm contracts and flattens
B1: the volume of the thorax increases, so the pressure inside it decreases
B1: air moves into the lungs because atmospheric pressure is now higher

long.q: Describe an experiment using limewater to show that expired air contains more carbon dioxide than inspired air.
scheme: B1: breathe in through a tube that draws air through one tube of limewater, and breathe out through a tube that bubbles air through a second tube of limewater
B1: the limewater that expired air passes through turns milky (cloudy) more quickly
B1: this shows expired air contains more carbon dioxide

long.q: Compare the percentages of oxygen and carbon dioxide in inspired and expired air, and explain the differences.
scheme: B1: expired air contains less oxygen than inspired air (about 16% compared with 21%)
B1: oxygen diffuses into the blood in the alveoli and is used in respiration
B1: expired air contains more carbon dioxide (about 4% compared with 0.04%)
B1: carbon dioxide is produced by respiration and diffuses from the blood into the alveoli

long.q: Explain why the rate and depth of breathing increase during exercise.
scheme: B1: muscles respire faster, producing more carbon dioxide
B1: the carbon dioxide concentration in the blood rises
B1: this is detected by the brain
B1: the brain sends more impulses to the intercostal muscles and diaphragm, increasing rate and depth so carbon dioxide is removed faster (and more oxygen taken in)

long.q: Explain how goblet cells and ciliated cells protect the gas exchange system.
scheme: B1: goblet cells make mucus
B1: mucus traps pathogens and dust particles
B1: cilia beat to move the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed

questions.q: What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
questions.why: Aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen.

questions.q: What is made by anaerobic respiration in human muscles?
questions.why: Without enough oxygen, muscles make lactic acid, creating an oxygen debt.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces…
questions.why: This is used in bread-making and brewing.

questions.q: Which is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some chose the photosynthesis equation, which is the reverse.

questions.q: Which statement best describes respiration?
o: Breathing air in and out of the lungs
Chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy
The exchange of gases across the alveoli
questions.why: Respiration is a set of chemical reactions in every living cell that releases energy for metabolism. Breathing and gas exchange are different processes.

long.q: Describe anaerobic respiration in human muscles during vigorous exercise and explain why breathing stays fast after exercise ends.
scheme: B1: glucose is broken down to lactic acid without oxygen
B1: releasing much less energy than aerobic respiration
B1: afterwards extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid (oxygen debt)

long.q: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans, stating word equations for each.
scheme: B1: aerobic equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ high energy release)
B1: anaerobic equation in muscles: glucose → lactic acid (+ low energy release)
B1: aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely, releasing much more energy per glucose molecule
B1: anaerobic respiration leads to an oxygen debt: lactic acid builds up in muscles and is later broken down in the liver using oxygen

long.q: State four uses of the energy released by respiration in the human body.
scheme: B1: muscle contraction
B1: protein synthesis
B1: cell division (or growth)
B1: one further use, e.g. active transport, passage of nerve impulses or maintaining a constant body temperature

long.q: State the word equation and the balanced chemical equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast, and explain how this process is useful in bread-making and in brewing.
scheme: B1: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
B1: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
B1: bread-making: the carbon dioxide produced makes the dough rise
B1: brewing: the ethanol produced is the alcohol in beer or wine

long.q: A student puts germinating peas in one vacuum flask and an equal mass of boiled, cooled peas in a second flask. Both sets of peas were first rinsed in dilute disinfectant. A thermometer is placed in each flask. Predict and explain the results, and explain why the peas were boiled and rinsed in disinfectant.
scheme: B1: the temperature rises in the flask with germinating peas but not (or much less) in the flask with boiled peas
B1: germinating peas respire, and respiration releases energy, some as heat
B1: boiled peas are dead and do not respire, so they act as a control showing the rise is caused by respiration of the living peas
B1: disinfectant kills microorganisms on the peas, which would otherwise respire and release heat

questions.q: Which organ makes urea?
questions.why: The liver breaks down excess amino acids (deamination), forming urea.

questions.q: What do the kidneys remove from the blood?
questions.why: Kidneys filter blood and reabsorb what's useful, excreting urea, water and salts as urine.

questions.q: Which organ removes urea from the blood?
questions.why: The liver makes urea by deamination; the kidneys excrete it.

questions.q: How is urea formed in the liver?
o: From the breakdown of old red blood cells
From the deamination of excess amino acids
questions.why: Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so the liver removes their nitrogen-containing part (deamination), which is converted to urea.

questions.q: In a healthy kidney, which substance is filtered out of the blood but then completely reabsorbed back into it?
questions.why: Glucose passes into the filtrate but is all reabsorbed in the tubule, so it is not normally in urine. Protein and red cells are too large to be filtered, and urea stays in the urine.

long.q: Define excretion and name two excretory products, stating the organ that removes each from the body.
scheme: B1: excretion is the removal of waste products of metabolism (toxic materials and substances in excess) from the body
B1: carbon dioxide, removed by the lungs
B1: urea (with excess water and ions), removed by the kidneys

long.q: Describe how urea is formed in the liver from excess amino acids.
scheme: B1: excess amino acids cannot be stored in the body
B1: in the liver they are deaminated
B1: deamination is the removal of the nitrogen-containing part of the amino acid
B1: this part is converted to urea, which passes into the blood and is excreted by the kidneys

long.q: Describe the route taken by urine from where it is made to where it leaves the body, naming each structure.
scheme: B1: urine is made in the kidneys
B1: it passes down the ureters
B1: it is stored in the bladder
B1: it leaves the body through the urethra

long.q: On a hot day a person produces a smaller volume of more concentrated urine. Explain why.
scheme: B1: more water is lost from the body in sweat
B1: so the kidneys reabsorb more water back into the blood
B1: so less water is left in the urine, giving a smaller volume of more concentrated urine

long.q: Healthy urine contains urea but no glucose and no protein. Explain how a kidney nephron produces urine with this composition.
scheme: B1: blood in the glomerulus is at high pressure, so small molecules such as water, glucose, urea and salts are filtered into the Bowman's capsule
B1: protein molecules (and blood cells) are too large to be filtered, so stay in the blood
B1: all the glucose is reabsorbed from the tubule back into the blood
B1: some water and salts are reabsorbed, according to the body's needs
B1: urea is not reabsorbed, so it remains in the urine with excess water and salts

questions.q: What is the correct order in a reflex arc?
o: Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
questions.why: Reflexes are fast, automatic responses through this pathway.

questions.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
questions.why: Insulin from the pancreas makes the liver store glucose as glycogen.

questions.q: In bright light, the pupil…
questions.why: Circular muscles of the iris contract, making the pupil smaller to protect the retina.

questions.q: A shoot bending towards light is called…
questions.why: Auxin collects on the shaded side, which grows more, bending the shoot to the light.

questions.q: Which is a difference between nervous and hormonal control?
o: Nervous responses are faster and shorter-lasting
Nerve impulses are carried in the blood plasma
questions.why: Nerve impulses travel quickly along neurones to a specific target and their effects are brief; hormones travel in the blood, act more slowly and their effects last longer.

long.q: A person touches a hot object and quickly pulls their hand away. Describe the pathway of the reflex arc involved.
scheme: B1: a receptor in the skin detects the stimulus (heat)
B1: a sensory neurone carries impulses to the spinal cord
B1: a relay neurone in the spinal cord passes impulses on
B1: a motor neurone carries impulses to the effector
B1: the effector, a muscle, contracts and moves the hand away

long.q: Describe how an impulse is passed from one neurone to the next across a synapse.
scheme: B1: an impulse arriving at the end of the first neurone causes vesicles to release neurotransmitter molecules
B1: the neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic gap
B1: it binds to receptor proteins on the membrane of the next neurone
B1: this stimulates an impulse in the next neurone
B1: synapses make sure impulses travel in one direction only

long.q: Explain how the eye changes to focus on a near object.
scheme: B1: the ciliary muscles contract
B1: the suspensory ligaments slacken
B1: the lens becomes more rounded (fatter)
B1: so light is refracted more and focused on the retina

long.q: Explain how the concentration of glucose in the blood is brought back to normal after a meal rich in carbohydrate.
scheme: B1: blood glucose concentration rises after the meal
B1: this is detected by the pancreas
B1: the pancreas secretes insulin into the blood
B1: insulin causes the liver (and muscles) to convert glucose into glycogen
B1: blood glucose falls back to the normal level: an example of negative feedback

long.q: Explain how auxin causes a plant shoot lit from one side to grow towards the light.
scheme: B1: auxin is made in the shoot tip
B1: auxin moves (diffuses) to the shaded side of the shoot
B1: auxin stimulates cell elongation on the shaded side
B1: the shaded side grows faster than the lit side, so the shoot bends towards the light (positive phototropism)

questions.q: What is a drug?
o: Any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
questions.why: This is the definition used in the syllabus; it includes medicines.

questions.q: Why should a course of antibiotics be finished?
o: To reduce the chance of resistant bacteria surviving
To make the next course stronger
questions.why: Stopping early lets the more resistant bacteria survive and multiply.

questions.q: Why should a full course of antibiotics be finished?
o: To make the next course cheaper
To kill all the bacteria and reduce the chance of resistant bacteria surviving
questions.why: Antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

questions.q: Which practice helps to reduce the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA?
o: Prescribing antibiotics for colds and flu
Giving antibiotics routinely to healthy farm animals
Using antibiotics only when they are really needed
Stopping antibiotics as soon as symptoms go
questions.why: Each use of an antibiotic selects for resistant bacteria, so using them only when essential (and finishing the course) slows the spread of resistance.

questions.q: Bacteria from a patient are grown on agar with paper discs of four antibiotics. The clear zones around the discs are: A 2 mm, B 15 mm, C 0 mm, D 8 mm. Which antibiotic should the doctor choose?
questions.why: The clear zone is where bacteria have been killed or stopped growing; the widest zone (B) shows the antibiotic these bacteria are most sensitive to. No zone (C) means they are resistant.

long.q: Define the term drug and describe how antibiotics are used in medicine.
scheme: B1: a drug is any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
B1: antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections
B1: they kill bacteria or stop them growing, without harming human cells

long.q: Explain why antibiotics can kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.
scheme: B1: antibiotics work by affecting structures or processes found only in bacterial cells, e.g. making the cell wall or bacterial enzymes
B1: viruses are not cells and have no cell wall or metabolism of their own
B1: viruses reproduce inside host cells using the host's processes, so there is nothing in the virus for the antibiotic to act on

long.q: Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic.
scheme: B1: a random mutation makes some bacteria resistant to the antibiotic
B1: when the antibiotic is used, the non-resistant bacteria are killed
B1: the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce
B1: they pass on the resistance, so over time most of the population is resistant (e.g. MRSA)

long.q: Suggest and explain how doctors and patients can limit the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria such as MRSA.
scheme: B1: doctors should prescribe antibiotics only when essential, e.g. not for viral infections or minor infections
B1: this means fewer bacteria are exposed to antibiotics, so there is less selection of resistant bacteria
B1: patients should complete the full course of antibiotics
B1: so that all the bacteria are killed and none survive to reproduce and spread resistance

long.q: A student spreads bacteria on an agar plate and places paper discs soaked in antibiotics A, B and C on it. After incubation the clear zones around the discs have diameters A = 12 mm, B = 24 mm and C = 0 mm. Identify the most effective antibiotic and explain what the result for C shows. State two safety precautions, and calculate the area of the clear zone around B (area = πr²).
scheme: B1: B is the most effective because it has the largest clear zone, so it killed or stopped the growth of most bacteria
B1: C has no clear zone, so the bacteria are resistant to antibiotic C
B1: one precaution, e.g. sterilise equipment / flame the forceps; tape the lid on but do not seal it completely
B1: a second precaution, e.g. incubate at 25 °C rather than 37 °C so that human pathogens are less likely to grow; do not open the plate after incubation
M1: radius = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 mm, area = π × 12²
A1: 452 mm²

questions.q: What is the main advantage of sexual reproduction?
questions.why: Variation helps a population survive changes in the environment.

questions.q: Where does fertilisation usually happen in humans?
questions.why: The sperm meets the egg in the oviduct.

questions.q: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
questions.why: Pollen is made in the anthers, on the filaments of the stamens.

questions.q: What is the function of the placenta?
o: It exchanges oxygen, nutrients and wastes between the mother's and the fetus's blood without them mixing
It lets the mother's blood flow directly into the fetus
It produces the eggs for the next pregnancy
It stops every substance in the mother's blood reaching the fetus
questions.why: The placenta brings the two blood supplies close together so substances diffuse across, while keeping them separate. Some harmful substances and pathogens can still cross.

questions.q: Which features are typical of an insect-pollinated flower?
o: Feathery stigmas hanging outside the flower
Small, light, smooth pollen made in huge amounts
Large, brightly coloured petals, scent and nectar
No petals and long, dangling anthers
questions.why: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects with colourful petals, scent and nectar. The other features belong to wind-pollinated flowers.

long.q: Compare asexual reproduction with sexual reproduction.
scheme: B1: asexual reproduction involves only one parent
B1: asexual offspring are genetically identical to the parent and to each other
B1: sexual reproduction involves the fusion of the nuclei of two gametes to form a zygote
B1: sexual offspring are genetically different from each other and from the parents

long.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of sexual reproduction to a population of wild plants and to farmers growing a crop.
scheme: B1: advantage: it produces variation, so some individuals may survive a change in the environment or a new disease
B1: advantage: variation allows the species to adapt by natural selection
B1: disadvantage: it is slower and needs two parents, so pollination or a mate is needed
B1: disadvantage for crops: offspring are not identical, so useful features of a good crop plant may be lost

long.q: Describe how the flowers of a wind-pollinated plant differ from those of an insect-pollinated plant.
scheme: B1: wind-pollinated flowers have anthers hanging outside the flower so pollen is blown away
B1: wind-pollinated flowers have large, feathery stigmas outside the flower to catch pollen
B1: wind-pollinated flowers make large amounts of small, light, smooth pollen
B1: insect-pollinated flowers have large, brightly coloured petals, scent and nectar to attract insects (wind-pollinated flowers do not)

long.q: Explain the roles of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in controlling the menstrual cycle.
scheme: B1: FSH from the pituitary gland stimulates an egg to develop in a follicle in the ovary
B1: oestrogen from the ovary causes the lining of the uterus to build up again
B1: a surge of LH from the pituitary gland causes ovulation (around day 14)
B1: progesterone from the empty follicle (corpus luteum) maintains the uterus lining
B1: if the egg is not fertilised, progesterone falls and the lining breaks down (menstruation)

long.q: Describe an experiment to show that seeds need water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to germinate.
scheme: B1: put the same number and type of seeds on cotton wool in each of several tubes, leave for a few days, then count how many have germinated
B1: control tube: moist cotton wool, open to the air, kept warm (about 20–25 °C)
B1: no water: seeds on dry cotton wool, open to the air, kept warm
B1: no oxygen: seeds in boiled, cooled water covered with a layer of oil (or a sealed tube with a chemical that absorbs oxygen), kept warm
B1: low temperature: moist cotton wool with air, kept in a refrigerator (about 4 °C)
B1: seeds germinate only in the control, showing all three conditions are needed

questions.q: Two heterozygous parents (Tt) are crossed. What fraction of offspring show the recessive phenotype?
questions.why: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt: one in four is tt.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are in a human gamete?
questions.why: Gametes are haploid: 23 chromosomes, half the body-cell number.

questions.q: What type of cell division makes gametes?
questions.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and gives genetic variation.

questions.q: Which sex chromosomes does a human male have?
questions.why: Males are XY and females XX.

questions.q: In mice, black fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). A black mouse is crossed with a white mouse and half of the offspring are white. What is the black mouse's genotype?
o: It cannot be told from this cross
questions.why: White offspring (bb) need a b allele from each parent, so the black parent must carry b and be Bb. Bb × bb gives a 1 : 1 ratio of black to white.

long.q: In pea plants the allele for tall (T) is dominant to the allele for short (t). Two heterozygous tall plants are crossed. Use a genetic diagram to find the expected percentage of short offspring.
scheme: B1: parents Tt × Tt
B1: gametes T and t from each parent
B1: offspring TT, Tt, Tt, tt
B1: 1 in 4 short: 25%

long.q: Define the terms gene and allele, and explain the difference between genotype and phenotype.
scheme: B1: gene: a length of DNA that codes for a protein
B1: allele: an alternative form of a gene
B1: genotype: the genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present (e.g. Tt)
B1: phenotype: the observable features of an organism (e.g. tall)

long.q: Describe how the base sequence of a gene controls the protein that a cell makes.
scheme: B1: the gene stays in the nucleus, and an mRNA copy of the gene is made
B1: the mRNA moves out of the nucleus to a ribosome in the cytoplasm
B1: the ribosome assembles amino acids into a protein in the order set by the mRNA
B1: each sequence of three bases codes for one amino acid
B1: the order of amino acids determines the shape and so the function of the protein

long.q: Compare mitosis and meiosis in humans.
scheme: B1: mitosis produces genetically identical cells
B1: meiosis produces genetically different cells
B1: mitosis produces diploid cells, with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell (46)
B1: meiosis produces haploid cells with half the number of chromosomes (23)
B1: mitosis is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction; meiosis produces gametes

long.q: The ABO blood group gene has three alleles: Iᴬ, Iᴮ and Iᴼ. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant and both are dominant to Iᴼ. A man with genotype IᴬIᴼ and a woman with genotype IᴮIᴼ have a child. Use a genetic diagram to show the possible blood groups of the child and state the probability that the child has blood group O.
scheme: B1: gametes: Iᴬ and Iᴼ from the man; Iᴮ and Iᴼ from the woman
B1: offspring genotypes: IᴬIᴮ, IᴬIᴼ, IᴮIᴼ, IᴼIᴼ
B1: phenotypes: AB, A, B and O
B1: blood group AB results because Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant, so both are expressed
B1: probability of blood group O = 1 in 4 (0.25)

long.q: Red-green colour blindness is caused by a recessive allele (Xᵇ) on the X chromosome. A woman with normal vision whose father was colour blind has children with a man with normal vision. Use a genetic diagram to find the probability that one of their sons is colour blind, and explain why none of their daughters will be colour blind.
scheme: B1: the woman is XᴮXᵇ, because she must have received Xᵇ from her father
B1: the man is XᴮY
B1: offspring: XᴮXᴮ, XᴮXᵇ, XᴮY, XᵇY
B1: probability that a son is colour blind = 1 in 2 (50%)
B1: every daughter receives Xᴮ from her father, so she has at least one dominant allele

questions.q: Which is an example of continuous variation?
o: Eye colour in a simple cross
questions.why: Height has a range of values, influenced by genes and environment.

questions.q: What is the source of all new alleles?
questions.why: Mutation creates new alleles; meiosis and fertilisation shuffle existing ones.

questions.q: How do bacteria become resistant to antibiotics?
o: Resistant mutants survive and reproduce (natural selection)
Antibiotics change their DNA on purpose
questions.why: Antibiotics kill non-resistant bacteria; resistant ones survive and pass on the allele.

questions.q: Which describes artificial selection?
o: The best-adapted organisms in the wild survive and reproduce
Humans choose individuals with useful features and breed only from them
A gene from one species is inserted into another
questions.why: In artificial (selective) breeding, people decide which individuals reproduce, over many generations. Survival of the best adapted in the wild is natural selection.

questions.q: Which feature helps a cactus reduce water loss in a desert?
o: Large, thin leaves with many stomata
Stomata on the upper surface exposed to the wind
Leaves reduced to spines, giving a small surface area
questions.why: Spines give a very small surface area for transpiration. Xerophytes also have thick waxy cuticles and few stomata, so the other options would increase water loss.

long.q: Describe the differences between continuous and discontinuous variation, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: continuous variation gives a range of phenotypes between two extremes
B1: example of continuous variation, e.g. body length or body mass
B1: discontinuous variation gives a limited number of distinct phenotypes with no intermediates
B1: example of discontinuous variation, e.g. ABO blood group or seed shape in peas

long.q: Explain how natural selection could lead to a population of rabbits living in a cold region having thicker fur over many generations.
scheme: B1: there is genetic variation in fur thickness within the population
B1: more rabbits are produced than the environment can support, so there is competition / a struggle for survival
B1: rabbits with thicker fur are better adapted and more likely to survive the cold
B1: they reproduce and pass on their alleles for thick fur to their offspring
B1: over many generations the frequency of these alleles increases in the population

long.q: Water lilies have large air spaces in their leaves and stems, stomata on the upper surface of their floating leaves, and very little xylem. Suggest how each of these features is an adaptation to life in water.
scheme: B1: air spaces help the leaves float near the light (and allow oxygen to diffuse to submerged parts)
B1: stomata on the upper surface are in contact with the air, so gas exchange can take place (the lower surface is under water)
B1: water supports the plant and is easily available, so little xylem (support and water-transport tissue) is needed

long.q: Describe how a farmer could use selective breeding to produce cows that give a higher milk yield.
scheme: B1: select cows with the highest milk yield
B1: breed them with a bull whose mother had a high milk yield
B1: select the female offspring with the highest milk yield and breed from them
B1: repeat over many generations

long.q: Define mutation, state two factors that increase the rate of mutation, and explain how a gene mutation can change the protein produced.
scheme: B1: a mutation is a genetic change (a random change in the base sequence of DNA)
B1: ionising radiation
B1: some chemicals (e.g. chemicals in tobacco smoke)
B1: a change in the base sequence changes the sequence of amino acids in the protein
B1: this can change the shape of the protein so it may not work properly

questions.q: In a food chain, what do the arrows show?
questions.why: Arrows point from the organism eaten to the one that eats it: the direction of energy flow.

questions.q: Why is energy lost at each trophic level?
o: It is used in respiration and lost as heat, movement and waste
questions.why: Only about 10% passes to the next level; the rest is used or lost.

questions.q: Which process returns carbon dioxide to the air?
questions.why: Respiration (and combustion and decomposition) release CO₂; photosynthesis removes it.

questions.q: The producers in a food chain contain 20 000 kJ of energy and the primary consumers contain 2000 kJ. What percentage of the energy was transferred?
questions.why: 2000 ÷ 20 000 × 100 = 10%. The other 90% was lost, for example as heat from respiration and in parts not eaten or not digested.

questions.q: In the nitrogen cycle, which organisms convert ammonium ions into nitrate ions in the soil?
questions.why: Nitrifying bacteria turn ammonium ions into nitrates that plants can absorb. Decomposers make ammonium from proteins, and denitrifying bacteria turn nitrates back into nitrogen gas.

long.q: In a grassland, the energy in the producers is 87 000 kJ m⁻² per year, in the primary consumers 9600 kJ m⁻² per year and in the secondary consumers 870 kJ m⁻² per year. Calculate the percentage efficiency of energy transfer from primary to secondary consumers and explain why so much energy is lost between trophic levels.
scheme: B1: energy is used in respiration and lost to the surroundings as heat
B1: not all parts of the organisms are eaten, and not all of what is eaten is digested (lost in faeces)
B1: energy is also lost in excretion (urine), so only a small fraction is passed on, which limits the number of trophic levels

long.q: Describe how carbon is cycled between the atmosphere and living organisms.
scheme: B1: plants remove carbon dioxide from the air by photosynthesis
B1: carbon compounds pass to animals when they eat plants (feeding)
B1: plants and animals return carbon dioxide to the air by respiration
B1: decomposers break down dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon dioxide by respiration
B1: combustion of fossil fuels (formed from dead organisms) releases carbon dioxide

long.q: Describe the roles of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle.
scheme: B1: nitrogen-fixing bacteria (in root nodules or soil) convert nitrogen gas into compounds such as ammonium ions
B1: decomposers break down proteins and urea in dead organisms and waste into ammonium ions
B1: nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium ions into nitrate ions
B1: denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate ions back into nitrogen gas
B1: plants absorb nitrate ions to make amino acids and proteins

long.q: A student wants to estimate the number of daisy plants in a field measuring 50 m by 20 m using a 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrat. Describe how the student should sample the field. The mean number of daisies per quadrat was 3.2. Estimate the number of daisies in the field.
scheme: B1: place the quadrat at random positions, e.g. using random numbers as coordinates on a grid
B1: count the daisies inside each quadrat
B1: use many quadrats (e.g. at least 10) and calculate the mean per quadrat
M1: area of a quadrat = 0.25 m², so mean per m² = 3.2 ÷ 0.25 = 12.8
M1: area of field = 50 × 20 = 1000 m²

long.q: A small number of yeast cells are added to a flask of sugar solution. Describe and explain the shape of the population growth curve over the following days.
scheme: B1: lag phase: slow growth at first, as there are few cells reproducing and they are adjusting to the conditions
B1: exponential (log) phase: rapid increase, as food is plentiful and there are few limiting factors
B1: stationary phase: the population stays constant because birth rate equals death rate
B1: this is caused by limiting factors such as shortage of sugar or build-up of toxic waste (ethanol)
B1: death phase: the population falls as the death rate exceeds the birth rate

questions.q: What can happen when fertiliser runs into a lake?
o: Eutrophication: algae bloom, then decay uses up oxygen
questions.why: Excess nitrates cause algal growth; bacteria decomposing dead algae use up the oxygen.

questions.q: Why does deforestation increase carbon dioxide in the air?
o: Less photosynthesis, and burning or decay releases CO₂
questions.why: Fewer trees take in CO₂, and burned or rotting wood releases it.

questions.q: Why can fertiliser running into a lake kill fish?
o: It makes the water too warm
Algae grow, die and are decomposed by bacteria that use up the oxygen
questions.why: This is eutrophication. Examiners (2023): candidates confused water pollutants with air pollutants.

questions.q: Which is a negative effect of growing a large monoculture of one crop?
o: Biodiversity falls and pests of that crop can spread easily
More habitats are made for wild animals
questions.why: Large areas of a single crop support few other species and give pests of that crop plenty of food, so biodiversity falls and pesticide use often rises.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a seed bank?
o: To store seeds of many plant species so that endangered ones can be grown again if lost in the wild
questions.why: Seed banks conserve the genetic diversity of plants, including endangered species, so they can be regrown and reintroduced in future.

long.q: Explain how fertiliser washed into a lake can lead to the death of fish.
scheme: B1: nitrate ions from the fertiliser cause rapid growth of algae (and water plants)
B1: the algae cover the surface and block light
B1: plants below cannot photosynthesise, so they die
B1: decomposers (bacteria) increase in number and break down the dead plants
B1: the decomposers respire aerobically, using up dissolved oxygen
B1: fish die because there is not enough oxygen in the water

long.q: State four undesirable effects of deforestation.
scheme: B1: loss of habitats, reducing biodiversity (and possibly causing extinctions)
B1: soil erosion
B1: flooding
B1: increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere (less photosynthesis, and trees may be burned), contributing to climate change

long.q: Describe the negative impacts on the environment of large-scale monocultures of crop plants and of intensive livestock production.
scheme: B1: monocultures reduce biodiversity, as hedges and natural habitats are removed
B1: pests and diseases spread easily through a single crop, so more pesticides are used
B1: pesticides can kill other, non-target organisms
B1: intensive livestock produce large amounts of waste that can pollute water, and methane, a greenhouse gas
B1: land is cleared for animal feed, and diseases spread easily in crowded animals

long.q: Give two reasons why species become endangered and describe three methods used to conserve endangered species.
scheme: B1: one reason, e.g. habitat destruction or hunting
B1: a second different reason, e.g. pollution, introduced species or climate change
B1: monitoring and protecting the habitat (e.g. nature reserves, legal protection)
B1: captive breeding programmes, with release back into the wild
B1: a further method, e.g. seed banks, education programmes or reducing climate change

long.q: Explain how fish stocks in the sea can be managed so that fishing is sustainable.
scheme: B1: a sustainable resource is one that can be removed from the environment without running out
B1: fishing quotas limit the number or mass of fish that can be caught
B1: controls on net mesh size let young fish escape, so they reach breeding age
B1: one further method, e.g. closed seasons during breeding, protected areas where fishing is banned, or restocking

questions.q: Which organism is used to make bread rise?
questions.why: Yeast respires anaerobically, releasing carbon dioxide that makes dough rise.

questions.q: In genetic modification of bacteria to make insulin, what is used to cut DNA?
questions.why: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences, leaving sticky ends; ligase joins the pieces.

questions.q: Why are bacteria useful in biotechnology?
o: They reproduce quickly and have plasmids that are easy to modify
questions.why: Fast reproduction and plasmids make them easy to grow and engineer.

questions.q: Why is the enzyme pectinase added when making fruit juice?
o: It kills bacteria in the juice
It breaks down pectin in plant cell walls, so more juice is released and it is clearer
It adds vitamins to the juice
questions.why: Pectinase breaks down pectin, which helps hold plant cells together, so the fruit releases more juice and the juice is less cloudy.

questions.q: A human gene and a bacterial plasmid are both cut with the same restriction enzyme. Why does this help them join?
o: Both get complementary sticky ends that can pair up
It kills the bacterium so the plasmid can be removed
It makes the plasmid much larger
It removes all the bases from the gene
questions.why: The same restriction enzyme leaves matching single-stranded sticky ends, so the gene's bases pair with the plasmid's, and DNA ligase then joins them.

long.q: Explain why bacteria are useful in biotechnology and genetic modification.
scheme: B1: they reproduce rapidly
B1: they can make complex molecules (e.g. proteins)
B1: there are few ethical concerns over growing and manipulating them
B1: they contain plasmids, which can easily be used to carry new genes into them

long.q: Describe how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.
scheme: B1: the human insulin gene is cut out of human DNA using a restriction enzyme
B1: this leaves sticky ends
B1: a bacterial plasmid is cut with the same restriction enzyme, giving complementary sticky ends
B1: the insulin gene and plasmid are joined by DNA ligase, forming a recombinant plasmid
B1: the recombinant plasmid is inserted into bacteria
B1: the bacteria multiply (e.g. in a fermenter) and express the gene, producing human insulin

long.q: Describe and explain the conditions that are controlled in an industrial fermenter used to grow microorganisms.
scheme: B1: temperature is controlled (e.g. a water jacket removes heat from respiration) to keep enzymes at their optimum
B1: pH is monitored and controlled so enzymes work at their optimum
B1: sterile air supplies oxygen for aerobic respiration
B1: nutrients are supplied for energy and growth
B1: the fermenter is sterilised (aseptic precautions) to prevent contamination by other microorganisms

long.q: Explain how biological washing powders remove stains, and why they are effective at low temperatures.
scheme: B1: they contain enzymes such as proteases and lipases
B1: these break down insoluble stains (proteins and fats) into small soluble molecules that wash away
B1: the enzymes work well at low temperatures, saving energy (high temperatures would denature them)

long.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of growing genetically modified crops.
scheme: B1: advantage: crops resistant to insect pests, so less insecticide spraying is needed
B1: advantage: crops resistant to herbicides, so weeds can be controlled without killing the crop
B1: advantage: crops with extra nutrients (e.g. vitamin A in Golden Rice) or higher yields
B1: disadvantage: GM seeds are expensive and farmers may have to buy new seed each year
B1: disadvantage: genes may spread to wild plants (e.g. herbicide-resistant weeds), or biodiversity may fall
